items.prose: A desk is long 300 six-month £100 calls on one share each: $S = \text{£}100$, $r = 5\%$, $\sigma = 20\%$. `bs_greeks` gives vega 27.36 for each, per 1.00 of vol. Overnight, implied vol falls two points.
items.question: About how much does the book lose from vega?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Convert vega to £ per vol point, then multiply by the points and the options.

byKey.per-unit: You used vega per 1.00 of vol. Two points is 0.02, so each call loses $27.36 \times 0.02$.
byKey.one-point: That is one point's loss. Vol fell two points.

explain.text: Per vol point each call moves $27.36 \times 0.01 = 0.2736$. Two points on 300 calls is $300 \times 0.2736 \times 2 \approx \text{£}164.15$.

items.prose: A pricer you cannot differentiate returns these prices for our one-year £100 call, at three share prices.
items.question: What delta does the central difference with $h = \text{£}1$ give?

feedback.correct: 0.6368, matching the closed form to four places.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the price at £101 minus the price at £99, over $2h$.

byKey.forward: You used the one-sided difference from £100 to £101. It errs like $h$; the central one like $h^2$.
byKey.no-half: You divided by $h$, not $2h$. The two prices are £2 apart.

explain.text: $(11.0967 - 9.8232)/2 = 0.6368$, against 0.6461 for the one-sided chord. The central chord cancels the curvature term, so even $h = \text{£}1$ gives four places.

items.prose: A colleague computes gamma for the same call with $h = 10^{-7}$ and gets $-0.71$. The closed form says 0.0188.
items.question: What went wrong?

options.text: The three prices agree to about 15 digits, so their difference is mostly rounding, divided by $h^2 = 10^{-14}$
The bump is too large, so the chord smooths the curvature away
options.why: Large bumps err like $h^2$. At $10^{-7}$ that error is negligible; the trouble is the other end.

options.text: The second difference is the wrong formula for gamma
options.why: The formula is right: at $h = \text{£}0.01$ it gives 0.018762.

options.text: Gamma of a long call can be negative near the money
options.why: A long call's price is convex in $S$, so its gamma is never negative.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what dividing by $10^{-14}$ does to tiny errors.

byKey.trunc: You blamed truncation. That error shrinks with $h$; the error that grows as $h$ shrinks is rounding.

explain.text: Each price carries a rounding error near $10^{-15}$. Divided by $h^2 = 10^{-14}$, that becomes an error of order 0.1 to 1. The dashboard's £0.01 bump sits between the two failures.

items.prose: Our one-year £100 put has delta $-0.3632$, gamma 0.018762, vega 37.52 per 1.00 and theta $-1.658$ a year. In one day the share falls £3 and implied vol rises two points.
items.question: What P&L does the four-term explain give?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $\Delta\,dS$, $\tfrac12\Gamma\,dS^2$, vega $d\sigma$ and $\Theta\,dt$, with $dt = 1/365$.

byKey.no-gamma: You left out the gamma term, $\tfrac12 \times 0.018762 \times 9 = 0.0844$.
byKey.theta-year: You charged a whole year of theta. One day is $1.658/365$.

explain.text: Delta earns $-0.3632 \times -3 = 1.0895$, gamma 0.0844, vega $37.52 \times 0.02 = 0.7505$, theta $-0.0045$. The total is £1.9199; revaluation gives £1.9302, a residual of 0.0104 from vanna and higher orders.

items.prose: Two at-the-money £100 calls on the same share, $r = 5\%$, $\sigma = 20\%$. With one year left gamma is 0.018762; with three months left it is 0.039288.
items.question: What rule of thumb does the ratio of the two gammas match?

options.text: Gamma grows like $1/\sqrt{T}$: a quarter of the time, about twice the gamma
Gamma grows like $1/T$: a quarter of the time, four times the gamma
Gamma does not depend on time to expiry
options.why: The two gammas differ by a factor of about 2.

options.text: Gamma shrinks as expiry nears, like vega
options.why: Vega shrinks like $\sqrt{T}$. Gamma moves the other way.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the two gammas and compare with 4 and with 2.

byKey.lin: You scaled gamma with $1/T$. The ratio is 2.09, which is $1/\sqrt{T}$ scaling.

explain.text: At the money gamma is about $\varphi(d_1)/(S\sigma\sqrt{T})$, so a quarter of the time roughly doubles it. The rate and $d_1$ move a little with $T$, which is why the ratio is 2.09 rather than exactly 2.

items.prose: Calls at one expiry, after cleaning dropped the £100 strike: £12.10 at £90, £9.40 at £95 and £2.90 at £105.
items.question: By how much does the £95 call sit above the chord between its neighbours?

feedback.correct: £0.3667 above the chord: a butterfly failure.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Weight the nearer neighbour more: $w = (105 - 95)/(105 - 90)$.

byKey.equal: You gave both neighbours weight one half. £95 is a third of the way from £90 to £105, so £90 gets $\tfrac23$.
byKey.swapped: You put the larger weight on the far neighbour. The nearer strike, £90, gets $w = \tfrac23$.

explain.text: The chord at £95 is $\tfrac23 \times 12.10 + \tfrac13 \times 2.90 = 9.0333$. The quote sits 0.3667 above it, so the prices are not convex there. `butterfly_violations` reports twice that, 0.7333, in its butterfly units.

items.prose: At the forward, the one-month vol is 25% and the two-month vol is 17%.
items.question: Is this a calendar arbitrage?

options.text: Yes: total variance falls from 0.00521 to 0.00482
No: an inverted term structure is normal after a scare
options.why: Inverted vol is allowed. Here total variance $\sigma^2 T$ falls as well, which is not.

options.text: No: an eight-point drop is too small to matter
options.why: The size of the vol drop is not the test. Compare $\sigma^2 T$ at the two expiries.

options.text: Yes: vol must never fall with expiry
options.why: Vol may fall with expiry. What must not fall is total variance.

feedback.correct: Total variance falls, so the forward variance is negative.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $\sigma^2 T$ for each expiry and compare.

byKey.no-vol: You checked the vol curve. At one month $w = 0.25^2/12 = 0.00521$; at two months $0.17^2/6 = 0.00482$: it falls.

explain.text: $w$ is $0.0625/12 = 0.00521$ at one month and $0.0289/6 = 0.00482$ at two. The forward variance between them would be negative, so a two-month option is priced below a one-month one at the same $k$.

items.prose: You point the dashboard at Deribit. A BTC call's mid is 0.031 BTC, and the index price is 58,000 US dollars.
items.question: What price, in US dollars, should the implied-vol solver see?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the BTC price by the index price.

byKey.raw: That is still in BTC. The strike is in dollars, so the price must be too.

explain.text: Deribit quotes options in BTC, so $0.031 \times 58{,}000 = 1{,}798$ dollars. Feed the solver 0.031 against a dollar strike and every implied vol collapses towards zero.
